newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal reopens battle over abortion.
newsitem.headline: Portugal reopens battle over abortion.

text.p: A bid in the Portuguese parliament to liberalise a 13-year-old abortion law is stoking old passions, with anti-abortionists and reformers clashing in the run-up to Thursday's vote.
"It could be the last chance to put Portugal on an equal footing with most of Europe," said Duarte Vilar, chairman of the state-financed Family Planning Association which backs reform.

Newspapers said on Wednesday that the vote, with the ruling Socialists and their main opposition not imposing a party line on deputies, was too close to call on two draft bills that would effectively allow abortions on demand in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.
A third bill extending the period when abortions can be carried out in cases of a deformed foetus, from the present 16 weeks to 24 weeks, looked set to pass, they said.
Abortion has been permitted in certain circumstances in Roman Catholic Portugal since 1984, a decade after young, leftist military officers put an end to 40 years of right-wing dictatorship.

Pregnancies can be ended at any time where the mother's life is at risk or during the first 12 weeks where her physical or psychological health could be severely impaired. The 12-week limit also covers rape victims.
But critics say that the law is ambiguous on the question of damage to a mother's health and that hospitals and doctors generally only terminate pregnancies in extreme cases.
The result is that the number of illegal terminations remains high, with bungled abortions being one of the major causes of maternal mortality in Portugal, Vilar said.
According to the Health Ministry only 275 legal abortions were carried out in 1995 in a country with a population of over 10 million people.
Illegal abortions could be running as high as 16,000 a year, Vilar said, although hospital officials dismiss the figure as an exaggeration.

Some indication of the likely numbers can be drawn from Spain where a similar law, but a more liberal interpretation by health authorities, led to some 49,000 legal abortions in 1995 in a population just three and a half times that of Portugal.
"The Spanish and Portuguese laws are virtually the same... the difference is in the way they are applied," said Vilar.

He said that he feared that if the reforms were not approved, it would reinforce the reluctance of Portuguese authorities to allow abortion even under existing rules, so boosting the number of illegal and risky terminations.
The two most controversial bills have been presented by the small Portuguese Communist Party and the Young Socialists, affiliated to the ruling party.
Besides lifting restrictions to abortion in the first three months, they would extend the period in cases of under-age rape to 16 weeks and include drug addicts in this category.

But anti-abortion groups have been fighting back, with Socialist Prime Minister Antonio Guterres, a practising Catholic, coming down firmly on the side of those opposing the Communist and Young Socialist bills.
He has been joined in the anti-reform camp by Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa, leader of the main opposition Social Democrats, and former premier Anibal Cavaco Silva.
Anti-abortion groups plan an all-night vigil outside a central Lisbon church followed by a march to parliament on Thursday.
